new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (32 pp., text layer present; the PDF's metadata gives the title 'PicDicIpiko1_narapela', SIL reapdata scan dated 2010). Page 4, 'Sounds and Spelling of Eva', reads exactly: 'There are 5 vowels: a e i o u / There are 13 consonants: b d g h k m n p r s t v ' / The s is a new sound for the language, and only occurs in words borrowed from other languages. / The ' (apostrophe) represents a consonant called a glottal stop.. e.g. u'opu \"nipa fruit\". / The r represents a sound which sometimes sounds like an English l.. / The words of Eva have different tones or tunes. This is not usually written, but if you want to you can underline a high tone, e.g. titi \"root\", titi \"design\".' the firs…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The compiler treats Eva (Ipiko) words as carrying lexically distinctive 'tones or tunes', illustrated by a minimal pair distinguished only by which syllable bears the high tone (ti.TI 'root' vs TI.ti 'design'); no statement about stress placement is made anywhere in the booklet.
new_statements.exceptions: None; tone is 'not usually written' in the orthography.
new_statements.domain_note: Orthography note in a community picture dictionary (word level, citation forms); not a phonological analysis. Whether the system is tone or a culminative pitch accent is not addressed. Rogers 2021 (LD&C SP24: 115-116) cites this same page as the only prosodic description of Ipiko.
new_statements.identity_note: Petterson 2007 describes the Eva dialect/variety of Ipiko (villages Ipiko, Pakemba on the Pie River and Nahoro on the Era River); he treats Ibigo, 'still spoken by a few people at Ipiko village', as a closely related lect. Glottolog ipik1244 has no dialect subdivisions; both Eva and Ibigo fall under ipik1244 / ISO ipo.
